pub fn dedup(&mut self)

Removes consecutive repeated elements in the vector according to the PartialEq trait implementation.

If the vector is sorted, this removes all duplicates.

§Examples

let mut vec = vec![1, 2, 2, 3, 2];

vec.dedup();

assert_eq!(vec, [1, 2, 3, 2]);

The parts of a Vec have the following invariants:

If size_of::<T>() and cap are non-zero, then:

ptr must point to the start of a memory block currently allocated via alloc.
Layout::array::<T>(cap) must fit the memory block of ptr. In particular, 
T must have the same alignment as the Layout ptr was allocated with, and
size_of::<T>() * cap must be at least the size of the Layout ptr was allocated with, and at most the size of the allocation returned the allocator.


size_of::<T>() * cap must be at most isize::MAX. See the safety documentation of pointer::offset.


If size_of::<T>() or cap is zero, then ptr must be any sufficiently aligned non-null pointer.

NOTE: ptr will not be passed to the allocator for deallocation by the destructor of Vec in this case. Thus, it is unwise to use a pointer acquired from the allocator for this, as overallocated memory may end up being leaked. Use ptr::dangling instead.
